[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Tutorial: Handling Missing Data in Pandas (NaN, None, NaT)"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Dealing with missing data is a fundamental skill in data science. In Pandas, missing data typically manifests in three ways: NaN (Not a Number) for floating-point data, None for object-dtype data, and NaT (Not a Time) for datetime data. This tutorial covers how to identify, drop, and fill missing values effectively."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Identifying Missing Data"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Before handling missing values, you need to locate them. Pandas provides the isnull() and notnull() methods to create boolean masks of the DataFrame."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Creating a sample DataFrame with NaN, None, and NaT
data = {
    'Name': ['Alice', 'Bob', None, 'David'],
    'Age': [25, np.nan, 30, 22],
    'Joined': [pd.NaT, pd.Timestamp('2021-01-01'), pd.Timestamp('2022-05-10'), pd.NaT]
}

df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df.isnull())"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Dropping Missing Data"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"If your dataset is large or missing data is minimal, dropping rows or columns with missing values using dropna() is a viable option."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"# Drop any row that contains at least one missing value
clean_rows = df.dropna()
print(clean_rows)

# Drop any column that contains at least one missing value
clean_cols = df.dropna(axis=1)
print(clean_cols)"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Filling Missing Data"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Instead of deleting records, you can impute missing values using the fillna() method. You can substitute specific values, use statistical metrics like the mean, or apply forward/backward filling."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Constant filling: Replace all NaN values with a default string or number."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Column-specific filling: Pass a dictionary to target specific columns."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Method filling: Use methods like 'ffill' to propagate the last valid observation forward."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"# Fill missing Age with the mean Age, and Name with 'Unknown'
values = {'Age': df['Age'].mean(), 'Name': 'Unknown'}
df_filled = df.fillna(values)
print(df_filled)"},{"order":15,"type":"heading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"Proper management of NaN, None, and NaT ensures your machine learning models and data analysis pipelines do not throw unexpected errors. Always evaluate whether dropping or imputing missing data is the best strategy for your specific domain."}]
